4.Experimentalmethods
Thespecimenswerestoredforfiveyearsinamagneticallyshielded
roomwithanambientmagneticfieldintensityof∼0.2%oftheEarth's
field, allowing their unstable and unwanted viscous remanent
magnetization (VRM) components to substantially decay. Then the
specimens'residualnaturalremanentmagnetization(NRM)compo-
nentsweremeasuredusinganautomatedvertical-axis2GEnterprises
DC-SQUID magnetometer with a sensitivity of ∼2×10−6 A/m for a
standardspecimen.
Initiallyonespecimenpersitewasalternatingfield(AF)demag-
netizedin12stepsupto120mTusingaSapphireInstrumentsSI-4
demagnetizer, and two additional specimens were thermally (Th)
demagnetized in 14 steps up to 630 °C using a Magnetic Measure-
ments(MM-80)demagnetizer.Examiningtheresultsoftheseinitial
tests,afourthspecimenpersitewastestedbyfirstAFdemagnetizing

600 °C. Excluding 36 remaining specimens that had been glued
togetherandwere,therefore,AFdemagnetizedin10stepsto90mT,

5.Discussion
5.1.Apparentpolarwanderpath
The reference apparent polar wander path (APWP) for North
AmericaofBesseandCourtillot(2002)isusedfordatingtheChRMof
the Taylor Mountain batholith. The path (Fig. 10) is based on 221
paleopolesfromallcontinentsafterrotationintotheNorthAmerican
frame, runs from 200 Ma to present, and was calculated in 10 Ma
increments using a sliding window length of 20 Ma. The path was
extendedfrom200Mato230MaasproposedbyTanetal.(2007).The
statisticalsignificanceofdirectionalpopulationswasdeterminedusing
thetestofMcFaddenandLowes(1981).Howeverforthepurposeof
clarity,allthepaleopolesshowninFigs.10,11and12arecircumscribed
bytheir1σconeof63%confidenceratherthantheconventional2σcone
of95%confidence.Thisisbecausetwopaleopoles,orapaleopoleandan
APWP, are significantly different at 95% confidence to a close
approximationiftheir1σerrorlimitsdonotoverlap.

5.6.LateTriassic–JurassicYTTtectonics toenveloptheplateauxandtoclosewiththemagainsttheQuesnel
Tempelman-Kluit (1976), noting their similarity in lithology and
age, suggested that the Taylor Mountain batholith and related Late
Triassic–EarlyJurassicplutonsoftheYTTandtheKlotassinintrusions
oftheStikineterraneweretherootsofanislandarcformedalongthe
margin of the Stikine terrane. Next, Tempelman-Kluit (1979)
suggested that the Stikine terrane, with the YTT beneath, rifted
awayfromNorthAmericatoopentheAnvilOcean.Theoceanthen
closedtoformtheislandarcinLateTriassic,causingtheStikineand
YTT terranes to accrete to North America in the Middle Jurassic to
earliestCretaceousbyobductiononthrustfaults,whichtrappedthe
Slide Mountain and Cache Creek terranes in between (Tempelman-
Kluit,1979;Silberlingetal.,1992).
ThepresenceofTethyanfossilsofAsianaffinityintheCacheCreek
terraneamidterraneswithfossilsofNorthAmericanaffinity(Monger
andRoss,1971)andtheadventofplatetectonictheory,ledMonger
(1977)tosuggestthataseriesofallochthonouscrustalfragmentsor
microplatesofvariedoriginsaccretedsequentiallytoNorthAmerica
fromthesouthwesttoformtheCanadianCordillera(seealsoConey
etal.,1980;Mongeretal.,1982).Fosteretal.(1994)consideredtheYTT
subterrane containing the Taylor Mountain batholith to be such a
discretemicroplatethatlaytothenorthoftheStikinemicroplateprior
toaccretion.Morerecently,EnglishandJohnston(2005)interpreted
